black-d01.inserted:
Were PyPy 3.7 still among the interpreters _Black_ can run on, this caveat would still
  apply to current releases.

black-d03.inserted:
If a module still has to be importable by the old interpreter as well, where a `u`
marker does change the type of the literal, add `py27` to the `--target-version` values
you format it with and _Black_ will leave those markers alone.

black-d04.inserted:
- If your CI image is still on Python 3.7, installing `black` there will keep resolving
  to 23.3.0, the last release that runs on it; current releases need Python 3.10 or
  newer.

black-d05.inserted:
As the first release of 2026, this is the one upgrade this year that is expected to
change how already formatted code looks: plan for a single reformatting commit when you
move to it, after which later 26.x releases will leave that code as it is (the
`--preview` and `--unstable` styles excepted).

black-d06.inserted:
Because the watcher always runs whatever `black` sits at the configured path, upgrading
that installation shows up on the very next save: after any upgrade, even to a bugfix
release, expect files you had already formatted to come back with a few changed lines
you never touched, and commit that churn separately from your own edits.

black-d07.inserted:
Long string literals are the most common case, because _Black_ does not split them in
its default style. Run it with `--preview` and expect those strings to be broken into
implicitly concatenated pieces that fit your limit as well.

click-d02.inserted:
If Click still supported Python 2, where the plain `str` type held bytes, this
point would need a much longer explanation. On the Python 3 versions it does
support, text modes such as `'r'` give your command `str` and binary modes
such as `'rb'` give it `bytes`.

click-d03.inserted:
Keep that `None` in mind if you annotate the decorated function: a hint
written as `text: str | None` raises a `TypeError` as soon as the module is
imported on the older Python versions Click supports, so either spell it
`Optional[str]` or start the file with `from __future__ import annotations`.

click-d04.inserted:
- If your install instructions still set the completion variable to the
  pre-8.0 value `source_zsh`, change it to `zsh_source` and regenerate the
  script so that users actually receive the fix above.

click-d06.inserted:
If most of your users work in Windows Terminal, expect them to get no tab
completion from the classes below until you write a {class}`ShellComplete`
subclass for their shell and register it with {func}`add_completion_class`.

click-d07.inserted:
If `cli` is instead a {class}`CommandCollection` that merges several plugin
groups, create `test` and `dist` with `@click.command()` on one of its source
groups rather than with `@cli.command()`, and add that group with
{meth}`~CommandCollection.add_source`. `ctx.forward` and `ctx.invoke` then
work unchanged.

click-d08.inserted:
- A Windows application frozen with PyInstaller or a similar tool no
  longer needs to bundle a separate console-color package next to Click for
  styled output; the terminal renders the escape codes itself.

flask-d02.inserted:
In a deployed application you don't want to rely on someone running this by
hand. Register ``init_db`` in your application module as the hook Flask calls
once, just before it dispatches the very first request, so the tables exist
before any view touches ``db_session``.

flask-d03.inserted:
So while you are working on a handler for 500 errors with ``flask run``, start
the server without the ``--debug`` option when you want to see your page; with
the option on, the debugger takes its place.

flask-d04.inserted:
If you connect receivers to Flask's :data:`.request_started` and
:data:`.request_tearing_down` signals instead, expect bug reports of
``init_app`` failing with a ``RuntimeError`` on some users' machines but not
on yours, depending on what else is installed in their virtualenv. Catching
that error and falling back to the decorator methods above keeps the
extension working for them.

flask-d06.inserted:
For example, a :file:`.flaskenv` that puts the project in the development
environment gives everyone who checks it out the reloader and debugger, while
a :file:`.env` on a staging server only has to set the environment back to
``production`` to switch them off again.

flask-d07.inserted:
Were blueprints still able to register a hook that runs only before the
application's first request, a blueprint mounted twice would also have had to
decide whether that hook should run once or once per registration.

flask-d08.inserted:
If you are porting an API like this from an older Flask release that tuned
its ``jsonify`` output with ``JSON_``-prefixed keys in ``app.config``, set the
matching attributes on ``app.json`` instead, such as ``app.json.sort_keys``;
current Flask no longer reads those config keys.

httpx-d01.inserted: Had the old default been kept, a client like that would have gone on doubling its traffic indefinitely, with the misconfiguration only visible to someone who thought to look at `response.history`.

httpx-d02.inserted: If you are still on an HTTPX release older than 0.20, where redirects were followed automatically, bear in mind that each request in a redirect chain is given its own timeout, so a single call that gets redirected a few times can take correspondingly longer than that before it finally raises.

httpx-d03.inserted: One thing to keep in mind: if the URL you pass to `client.get(...)` answers with a redirect, the `Content-Type` charset used here is the one sent by the page at the end of the redirect chain, not by the URL you originally requested.

httpx-d04.inserted: You'll only need to write out transports like this once the rules depend on more than the scheme. A client that simply sends `http://` and `https://` traffic to two different proxies can still be handed the two proxy URLs directly, keyed by scheme, and it will build the equivalent mounts for you.

httpx-d05.inserted:
Or, with a single parameter:

```pycon
>>> r = httpx.get('https://httpbin.org/redirect-to', params={'url': '/get'})
>>> r.url
URL('https://httpbin.org/get')
```

httpx-d06.inserted: To check that an old link which now redirects still resolves to a working page, request the old URL as usual and chain `.raise_for_status()` onto it in the same way.

httpx-d08.inserted: Code that still constructs a client with `app=...` will now fail with a `TypeError` as soon as the client is instantiated; pass the application through `transport=httpx.WSGITransport(app=...)` or `transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=...)` instead.

pip-d02.inserted: Had pip still been running its pre-2020 resolver by default, the recursive, one-dependency-after-another picture in several of the answers below would have been a fair description of what pip does; with the backtracking resolver, pip may go back and swap out a version it has already picked when a later requirement conflicts with it.

pip-d03.inserted:
Because PyPI no longer answers ``pip search`` queries, checking for newer
   releases from the terminal means using ``--outdated`` (or :ref:`pip index`),
   which reads the same index pages as ``pip install`` does.

pip-d04.inserted:
For example, with ``python3.9 -m pip download --only-binary=:all: numpy``
the ``cp39`` wheels are the relevant links, and wheels built for other CPython
versions are skipped.

pip-d05.inserted: If you are still passing `--use-deprecated=legacy-resolver` in your own workflows, bear in mind that the legacy resolver is deprecated and unsupported, so the `--force-reinstall` behaviour you see with it may not match what is described or recommended here.

pip-d06.inserted:
``search`` sits directly under ``Command`` because it never builds a
``PackageFinder`` or reads Simple API pages: it sends a single query to the
index's search API and prints the names and summaries that come back, so a
bare ``pip search <term>`` with no ``--index`` option simply lists the
matching projects.

pip-d07.inserted:
If you do build a locking tool on top of `--report`, validate the `install` array
before writing a lock: for each item, evaluate its `requires_dist` entries against the
`environment` markers, check that the version recorded for every dependency they name
satisfies them, and refuse to lock when one does not, since the report keeps the first
version pip settled on for a shared dependency even when a requirement it reached later
asked for a different one.

pip-d08.inserted:
2. | When the package is a project in a local directory, expect the
        checkout to be left exactly as it was after
        ``pip install ./myproject`` -- there are no ``build/`` or
        ``.egg-info`` directories to add to ``.gitignore`` or clean up
        between builds.

poetry-d01.inserted: Were `poetry lock` to refresh every locked package on each run, a one-line change to `pyproject.toml` could produce a lock file diff touching most of your dependencies; keeping the existing versions keeps such diffs small and easy to review.

poetry-d03.inserted: If you want every dependency, not just one, moved to the newest version its constraint allows, keep the constraints as they are and run `poetry lock` followed by `poetry install` instead.

poetry-d04.inserted: On a machine where Poetry itself was installed with a Python 3.9 interpreter, for example the system Python of an older Linux distribution, the Poetry part of this output reports that 3.9 interpreter, independently of the Python version used by the project's virtual environment.

poetry-d05.inserted: Because the environment is activated in your current shell rather than in a nested one, leave it again with `deactivate`; typing `exit` would close that shell itself.

poetry-d06.inserted: If you are still on a 1.x release, the step to 2.0 is such a major version bump: on 1.x, `poetry export` works right after installing Poetry, while on 2.x it is only available once you have added the export plugin.

poetry-d07.inserted: You can see the effect of this registration on a freshly installed Poetry: `poetry list` already shows `export` among the available commands, next to the ones Poetry defines itself.

pytest-d01.inserted:
This form is also the simplest way to exercise a project against its oldest and newest
interpreters side by side: with pytest installed in each environment, ``python3.8 -m pytest``
and ``python3.13 -m pytest`` run the same suite under the same pytest release, so any
difference in the outcome comes from the interpreter rather than from pytest.

pytest-d02.inserted:
To try this out without touching the shared settings of a project that is configured
through ``pytest.toml``, put the same ``addopts`` line in an untracked ``pytest.ini`` in the
project root, and delete that file again once you are done.

pytest-d03.inserted:
If older tests in your suite still request :fixture:`tmpdir`, you can hand its value to
   helpers written for :fixture:`tmp_path` by wrapping it as ``pathlib.Path(tmpdir)``,
   which lets you migrate those tests one at a time.

pytest-d04.inserted:
If you port a ``setup_method``/``teardown_method`` pair to a fixture by
    turning it into a generator that yields the prepared state, expect the
    test to receive the generator object itself when the function is decorated
    with a plain ``@pytest.fixture``, and the code after the ``yield`` will
    never run as teardown.

pytest-d05.inserted:
If your repository root holds both a ``pytest.toml`` and a ``pytest.ini``, these two lines have
to go into ``pytest.toml``: that is the file pytest reads, and limits placed only in ``pytest.ini``
will leave the default of 8 lines or 640 characters in effect.

pytest-d07.inserted:
.. tab:: setup.cfg

    .. code-block:: ini

        # content of setup.cfg
        [pytest]
        markers =
            slow: marks tests as slow (deselect with '-m "not slow"')
            serial

pytest-d08.inserted:
Had pytest kept reading a bare ``[pytest]`` header from ``setup.cfg``, the ini
    snippet could have been pasted into that file as-is; since it does not, a
    ``setup.cfg`` needs the header ``[tool:pytest]`` instead.

requests-d01.inserted:
Don't count on those merged headers going out in the order you typed them,
though: on several of the Python versions Requests runs on, a plain ``dict``
does not remember insertion order, so if the server you are talking to cares
about header order, build both the session-level and the method-level headers
as ``collections.OrderedDict`` objects.

requests-d02.inserted:
-   If you are still running a 2.14.x release, it is this bundled copy
    that guesses response encodings: upgrading or removing a separately
    installed `chardet` package will not change what
    `r.apparent_encoding` reports.

requests-d04.inserted:
Every interpreter Requests supports today is 3.10 or newer, and 3.10
    removed the old ABC aliases from `collections` itself, so an adapter
    or auth plugin that still imports `Mapping` or `MutableMapping`
    straight from `collections` will fail to import next to current
    Requests; it needs the `collections.abc` spelling as well.

requests-d06.inserted:
Had Requests kept supporting Python 2, header keys would still come
    back as two different types depending on the interpreter; on the
    Python 3 versions it supports today they are always `str`.

requests-d07.inserted:
The quickest way to see what you would be subclassing is to read the code you
already have: unzip the ``requests-<version>-py3.x.egg`` file in your
``site-packages`` directory and open ``requests/adapters.py`` inside it.

requests-d08.inserted:
That license covers Requests' own code only. The character-encoding detector
that is installed alongside it is distributed under the LGPL, so if you vendor
Requests into a closed-source application you will also need to ship that
library's source, or offer it on request, to stay within its terms.
